articles.title: Like a rhinestone cowgirl – Dolly Parton’s most glorious, joyful and meta looks
articles.summary: Across six decades, the late country singer and pop culture icon turned self‑presentation into a flamboyant art form. • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here.
body: Dolly Parton may have had a record 25 US country No 1 singles, released 66 studio albums and earned six Golden Globe nominations, among many other achievements, but the Tennessee-born star also had an incredible number of fashion moments. “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap”, she famously quipped when asked about her style. As we bid her farewell, six Guardian writers reflect on their favourite Dolly looks.

While Parton wore a plethora of looks, sometimes up to 10 a day, you always knew what you were going to get. For over 60 years she held firm to her signature style – a silhouette that emphasised her tiny waist, along with high heels, higher hair and a heavy sprinkling of sparkle. In today’s world of image architects and constant reinvention, her continuity felt even more refreshing.
points: Across six decades, the late country singer and pop culture icon turned self‑presentation into a flamboyant art form. • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox?

articles.title: How do you define good health – and achieve it – in a broken US medical system?
articles.summary: In a new book, Dr Lucy McBride aims to help us navigate US healthcare – and tread carefully in the wellness industry. Most of us want to be healthy, but it’s easier said than done. In the US, people are caught between a broken medical system and a well-resourced wellness industry.
body: Over 25 years of practicing medicine, running a primary care practice in Washington DC, Dr Lucy McBride has seen patients struggle to navigate the medical system.

In her new book, Beyond the Prescription, McBride presents a practical framework for getting the best results from a flawed system. It begins with defining what health means to you. For one person, it might be running ultramarathons and extending longevity at any cost; for another, it might be balance and the freedom to indulge.

“The relationship between a patient and their primary care doctor is, at its best, one of the most protective forces in human health – and, right now, we’re systematically dismantling it,” says McBride over Zoom.

It’s no wonder patients feel unheard, unsatisfied and lost. We spoke about how people can advocate for themselves and pursue their vision of health. Our conversation has been condensed and edited for clarity.
points: In a new book, Dr Lucy McBride aims to help us navigate US healthcare – and tread carefully in the wellness industry.

articles.title: I don’t get along with my sister-in-law. Should I try to address the dynamic? | Leading questions
articles.summary: There are two things to consider, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Are you hurt by the way she treats you or the way she sees you? I’m struggling with a dynamic with my sister-in-law. We’re not a natural fit personality-wise, and I’ve tried to be mindful of that.
body: There’s a recurring pattern where she corrects me quite sharply, with an impatience that often feels disproportionate or plain mean. She might snap while I am talking to her parents (with whom I have a good relationship), laugh at how I pronounce a placename, or dismiss a question as though it’s too stupid to answer. These interactions are quick and barely noticeable to anyone else, although my daughter and husband have both observed and agreed it was pretty mean.
I’m unsure how to interpret this behaviour. More importantly, I don’t know what I owe – to myself, to her, and to the wider family in terms of responding.

Is this best addressed directly, even at the risk of creating awkwardness? At what point does tolerating this kind of interaction become a failure to stand up for myself? And might there be a cost in not trying to improve a relationship that could otherwise be supportive as we navigate the more ordinary trials of family life – ageing parents, illness and difficult decisions?
points: There are two things to consider, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith.
Are you hurt by the way she treats you or the way she sees you?
I’m struggling with a dynamic with my sister-in-law.
We’re not a natural fit personality-wise, and I’ve tried to be mindful of that.
articles.author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith

articles.title: It’s time for all of us to get a grip and stop flaking on friends for no good reason
articles.summary: It has become normal to cancel on one another because we are so desperate to avoid even the most minor discomfort. It must cease immediately. It’s a Thursday night. You are sitting on the couch (the TV is on or you could be reading a book but most likely you are doom-scrolling).
body: Maybe this friend has been going through a rough time? Maybe they’ve got some exciting news about a perfect Hinge date (rare and shocking)? Maybe you’ve simply been “ships in the night” sailing through the capitalist rat race and miss each other’s company.

Either way, this hangout is premeditated and has been organised in advance with many exclamations of excitement. However, there is but one tiny problem: you no longer want to go. You are just … comfortable where you are.

You vaguely start calculating the hours left in the day – you might want to go to the gym in the morning (despite not having gone in weeks) and work was slightly strenuous today (you had to actually do your job).

You pick up your phone to text them something along the lines of “Massive day today – can we postpone? Maybe the weekend after next? Don’t wanna have a big one on a school night!” None of this is due to any sort of change of heart towards your pal: you simply can’t be bothered.

articles.title: Actually, Dining Side-by-Side in Restaurants Is Good
articles.summary: All this week, the Eater Today newsletter is dedicated to editor Hot Takes, a way to release the pressure valve of crankiness that comes with sweating your way through the end of summer. This story was previously published as part of that series.
body: I love the unspoken rules around dining out; admittedly, even more so when they make me feel like I’m earning a gold star for good decorum. I like dressing up for the occasion; I like waiting obediently at the host stand ( See? I’m not pushy like other diners ); and I enjoy the martyrdom role of reorganizing the table’s contents as the meal unfolds (distributing food if we’re sharing small plates, consolidating finished plates, pouring carafes).

My adherence to a certain kind of behavior around the rituals of dining, however, goes out the window when it comes to seating. Specifically, when the option arises for one kind of seating arrangement that’s usually deemed corny: dining side by side.

articles.title: From Personal Experience, These Are the Best Eyebrow Growth Serums
articles.summary: Yes, eyebrow growth serums actually work. From RevitaLash, Grande Cosmetics, The Ordinary, and more, discover the tried-and-true formulas for healthy, full arches.
body: As someone who was once ridiculed for her unibrow, it’s a shame that I virtually stand before you today to confess that I’ve fallen victim to over-tweezing my eyebrows. Quite the tragedy because my brows are such a prominent part of my face. Losing that much brow hair changed the way my entire face looks, and as a result, I’ve been on a mission to grow them back with the help of the best eyebrow growth serums.

Chockfull of nourishing ingredients that help condition the hair and support a healthy brow environment, these formulas can help sparse brows appear fuller and more defined over time. With consistent use, you may find yourself less dependent on brow pencils and pomades, or less tempted to turn to more permanent treatments like microblading or tinting, which aren’t always recommended by experts.

Thankfully, we’ve come a long way from the early aughts, when there was one very specific brow shape to aspire to. In 2026, you can embrace your natural brows, thin them out à la Gabriette, or go for a fuller look. And brow serums aren’t necessarily about achieving bushy, oversized brows, either. Many are simply designed to help you grow back what you’ve lost or fill in sparse areas.

articles.title: We Asked, You Answered: 2026 Summer Trends, Summarized
articles.summary: A look at our summer trend predictions and how we did, with input from the Vogue readers.
body: Let’s face it, summer is coming to a close. It’s time to take a look back at all the trends—hot or not—that bubbled up this season. To help us do so, we polled readers on Instagram and on our app, and looked at how Vogue stacked up when, at the top of summer, our staffers forecast which trends we thought we’d see most on the streets.

When we predicted summer trends earlier this year, Max Berlinger called out freaky flip-flops and he was vindicated—to a degree. Sandals did indeed get really wacky. Especially the barely-there hiking sandals that seemed to be everywhere. There were a lot of naked sandals—and exposed feet—this summer!

Meanwhile, with historic heatwaves scorching the globe, trying to find a way to wear less and still be stylish proved to be one of the season’s more difficult propositions. Enter sheer clothes, as Hannah Jackson predicted. See-through, breathable, opaque layers helped us all beat the heat and still look chic. Here’s how to wear them according to the street style set. Hilary Milnes foresaw a scarf girl summer, and she was right: Jackson tracked how celebrities wore the trend while Irene Kim kept an eye on the street style set.

articles.title: The Benefits of Walking for Longevity
articles.summary: The benefits of walking are well known, but research suggests that doing this simple, accessible exercise regularly may also help you live longer.
body: The secrets to living a long and healthy life can sometimes be easier than you’d expect. One of the simplest things you can do for longevity is to go for a walk.

Walking may be the easiest form of exercise. Collecting steps is uncomplicated and can be done anywhere: before or after a long day at the office, on the way to a bar, or before breakfast. You don’t need any extra equipment. Best of all, there’s no need to change outfits or shower afterward; you just need a comfy pair of shoes. Below, the experts break down all the benefits of walking and its effects on our overall health and longevity.

articles.title: Are Sulfate-Free Shampoos Actually Better? Vogue Investigates
articles.summary: Sulfate-free shampoos are the gold standard for gentle hair care, but are sulfates actually harmful? Here, experts break down the misconceptions and share their picks for the best sulfate-free shampoos.
body: Of the many beauty commandments we were taught (e.g., thou shall wear sunscreen every day; thou shall not sleep with wet hair, etc.), one that causes some confusion involves an ingredient that everyone has deemed a red flag in hair care: sulfates.

Sulfates are cleansing agents that attract oil, product buildup, and dirt. Often found as sodium lauryl sulfate or sodium laureth sulfate on product ingredient lists, the foaming surfactants are used in many shampoos to give your hair and scalp a very thorough cleanse. So, if they help clean hair, why are they so taboo?

It really all comes down to how harsh the ingredient can be in certain circumstances. “Sulfates aren’t inherently bad or dangerous, but they can be more cleansing and potentially more stripping on the hair,” says celebrity hairstylist Kennedy Trisler. “Along with removing dirt, oil, and product buildup, they can also remove some of the hair’s natural oils.”
